events.headline: RBI may hike repo rate to 6.25% by H1 2027, warns Deutsche Bank as inflation risks persist

items.title: RBI may hike repo rate to 6.25% by H1 2027, warns Deutsche Bank as inflation risks persist
items.summary: The bank expects 100-basis-point monetary tightening as inflationary pressures persist; rupee may weaken beyond 97 per US dollar.

events.article_text:
The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) may raise the repo rate to 6.25% by the first half of 2027, implying cumulative monetary tightening of 100 basis points in the current cycle, as persistent inflationary pressures and resilient economic growth could warrant a tighter monetary policy, according to a report by Deutsche Bank.

The bank expects the RBI to raise the policy rate by 25 basis points in December 2026, followed by another 50 basis points of tightening during the first half of 2027. The forecast is more hawkish than market expectations and reflects the possibility of economic growth remaining above 7% even as inflation stays elevated.

The RBI's monetary policy decisions will be closely watched as policymakers balance price stability with the need to sustain economic growth amid uncertainty in global energy markets.

Deutsche Bank expects consumer price index (CPI) inflation to average 6% in October-December 2026, 5% in FY27 and 4.7% in FY28.

The report flagged upside risks to inflation if domestic fuel prices are increased after Diwali. It also warned that wholesale price inflation exceeding 11% could result in higher input costs being passed on to consumers, adding to retail inflationary pressures.

Household inflation expectations have risen to 10% from 8% before the West Asia conflict, according to the report. The increase raises concerns about second-round effects, in which higher prices influence wage demands, business costs and future price-setting decisions.

These factors could complicate the RBI's efforts to bring inflation under control and strengthen the case for further monetary tightening.

Despite the inflation risks, Deutsche Bank expects India's real gross domestic product (GDP) growth to remain above 7% in both FY27 and FY28.

However, the report cautioned that economic momentum could moderate in the second half of FY27. Higher crude oil prices, a below-normal monsoon and an adverse base effect following the previous year's goods and services tax (GST) rate cuts could weigh on growth.

Higher energy costs could also increase pressure on businesses and households, potentially affecting consumption and investment.

The report highlighted continuing risks to the Indian rupee despite recent RBI measures that temporarily reduced dollar demand and helped the currency recover to around ₹94.50 against the US dollar.

India's foreign exchange reserves have declined by approximately $60 billion from their peak of $786 billion in early September.

Deutsche Bank expects the rupee to weaken beyond ₹97 per dollar during 2027 if the global macroeconomic environment does not improve meaningfully.

On the fiscal front, Deutsche Bank expects the Centre to meet its FY27 fiscal deficit target of 4.3% of GDP, supported by the RBI's dividend transfer and possible expenditure adjustments.

However, fiscal consolidation could become more difficult in FY28 because of elevated oil prices, higher subsidy requirements and the potential expenditure implications of the 8th Pay Commission.

The bank said maintaining price stability alongside financial stability would remain critical as India navigates external economic uncertainty.

analysis.tldr: Loans could become costlier as the central bank plans to raise interest rates to fight rising prices.
the_story: Deutsche Bank reported that the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) may raise the repo rate (the interest rate at which the central bank lends money to commercial banks) to 6.25% by the first half of 2027.

The forecast includes a 25 basis point (0.25 percentage point) hike in December 2026, followed by another 50 basis point hike in the first half of 2027, driven by persistent inflation and strong economic growth.
Consumer price index (CPI) inflation is expected to average 6% in October-December 2026, 5% in FY27, and 4.7% in FY28, with risks from fuel prices and wholesale price inflation exceeding 11%.
Household inflation expectations have risen to 10% from 8% before the West Asia conflict, risking second-round effects on wages and business costs.
The rupee faces ongoing risks and could weaken beyond ₹97 per US dollar during 2027, as India's foreign exchange reserves have declined by about $60 billion from their peak of $786 billion.
analysis.what_happened: Deutsche Bank issued a warning report stating that the RBI will likely need to raise its key lending rate to 6.25% by early 2027. This potential tightening is caused by stubborn inflation, rising household price expectations, and strong economic growth remaining above 7%, which force the central bank to cool down demand.
analysis.analogy: It is like a doctor prescribing a stricter diet and exercise plan because a person's body is working overtime and getting a bit too heated, requiring controlled cooling to stay healthy.
why_it_matters_india: Inflation stays elevated due to higher fuel costs and rising household expectations.
The RBI responds by raising the repo rate (the rate at which banks borrow from the central bank) to 6.25% to curb spending.
Commercial banks pass on these higher costs, making home, auto, and personal loans more expensive for ordinary people.
Meanwhile, high global energy costs and shrinking foreign exchange reserves put downward pressure on the Indian rupee.

impacts.target: Interest rates on home and car loans
impacts.rationale: Higher repo rates mean banks pay more to borrow money, passing those costs onto borrowers, which is bad for people paying off loans.
Lower foreign exchange reserves and global pressures could weaken the rupee beyond ₹97 per dollar, making imported goods like electronics and crude oil more expensive.
Monetary tightening is designed to bring inflation down from its forecasted peaks, which helps stabilize everyday living costs over time.

Changes in domestic fuel prices after Diwali
Movements in India's foreign exchange reserves
analysis.caveats: The forecasts depend heavily on global crude oil prices and whether the geopolitical situation in West Asia changes unexpectedly.

events.article_text:
Oil Prices Climb as Houthi Attacks Reignite Saudi Supply Fears

Josh Owens is the Content Director at Oilprice.com and a veteran energy journalist with over a decade of experience covering global energy markets and geopolitics.…

Oil prices climbed in early Asian trade on Wednesday as renewed Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia reignited supply fears in the region. Falling inventories and reports that the U.S. is preparing for a new military campaign against Iran after the midterm elections added to the upward momentum.

At the time of writing, Brent oil futures were trading at $115.70 per barrel, up 1.62% on the session, while West Texas Intermediate futures had risen 1.34% to trade at $101.20 per barrel.

The most recent gains came after a nearly $2 decline on Tuesday, a decline driven by hopes that the most recent round of diplomatic talks between Saudi, Turkish, Pakistani, and Iranian officials would bear fruit.

The most immediate concern for oil markets revolves around reports that Saudi Arabia's Ras Tanura complex has been targeted. The Houthis claimed on Tuesday that they had struck the 550,000-barrel-per-day Ras Tanura refinery with a ballistic missile.

At the time of writing, Saudi authorities have not confirmed a direct hit on the refinery, and there has been no independently verified evidence of extensive damage or a major interruption to operations.

Reports suggest that a fire near Saudi Aramco's facilities at Ras Tanura was contained following an attack in the region early Tuesday. The extent of any damage remains unclear.

While the details around the refinery attack are disputed, the broader wave of attacks has been well documented. Saudi officials reported intercepting three ballistic missiles aimed at the kingdom's Eastern Province and four drones directed toward southern Saudi Arabia on Tuesday. Saudi air defenses also intercepted two missiles targeting Riyadh, where falling debris damaged a building, a construction site and a vehicle, according to Saudi Civil Defense statements reported by the Associated Press.

Separately, the Houthis claimed a direct hit on Saudi Arabia's Defense Ministry in Riyadh and attacks on military aircraft; again, those claims have not been verified.

For oil markets, Ras Tanura remains the critical element of these latest attacks, as it combines substantial refining capacity with a critical export terminal on the Persian Gulf.

Concerns surrounding the latest attacks on Saudi Arabia have been compounded by a new report from the Wall Street Journal, which claims the United States has warned several Gulf Arab countries to prepare for the possibility of a short, intense military campaign after the November 3 U.S. midterm elections.

If nothing else, the latest round of attacks on Saudi Arabia and rumors of a new U.S.-Israel offensive on Iran suggest Monday’s diplomatic efforts have resulted in little to no progress in bringing peace to the region and resuming oil flows.

Meanwhile, U.S. inventory data offered additional support for crude prices, with the American Petroleum Institute estimating that crude inventories fell by approximately 2.03 million barrels in the week ending October 23. The bullish impact of that report was somewhat tempered by a rise in both gasoline inventories and distillate stocks.

Traders will now be watching Wednesday’s EIA inventory report closely for confirmation of those trends.

analysis.tldr: Rising global crude oil prices mean India will likely face costlier petrol, diesel, and imported goods, which can push up everyday inflation.
the_story: Oil prices climbed in early Asian trade on Wednesday, with Brent oil futures at $115.70 per barrel (up 1.62%) and West Texas Intermediate at $101.20 per barrel (up 1.34%).

The price jump was triggered by renewed Houthi attacks targeting Saudi Arabia—including a claimed missile strike on the 550,000-barrel-per-day Ras Tanura refinery complex—raising fears of oil supply disruptions.

Saudi officials reported intercepting multiple ballistic missiles and drones over the Eastern Province, Riyadh, and southern regions, though damage extent remains unclear and unconfirmed independently.

Upward pressure was also fueled by reports that the U.S. warned Gulf Arab countries to prepare for a potential military campaign against Iran, and U.S. data showing crude inventories fell by about 2.03 million barrels.
analysis.what_happened: Oil prices went up because rebel attacks in Saudi Arabia sparked worries that oil production and exports could get disrupted. This fear was made worse by shrinking oil stockpiles in the U.S. and growing political tensions involving the U.S. and Iran.
analysis.analogy: It is like a major bakery that supplies half your town suddenly facing a fire scare and security threats; even before knowing if the ovens are broken, the fear of fewer loaves makes everyone rush to buy, driving prices up.
why_it_matters_india: Global oil prices jump because of supply fears in Saudi Arabia.
India imports a vast majority of its crude oil needs from abroad.
More expensive oil means India has to spend more dollars to buy fuel, putting downward pressure on the rupee (each rupee buys fewer dollars).
Higher import bills feed into domestic inflation, raising costs for transport, manufacturing, and everyday goods.

impacts.target: Crude oil import cost for India
impacts.rationale: Global benchmark prices rose due to Middle East supply fears, directly increasing the cost for oil-importing countries like India—generally bad for consumers as it raises energy costs.
Costlier crude oil means India needs more US dollars to pay for fuel imports, which tends to weaken the rupee—generally bad because imported goods become more expensive.
When crude oil prices climb, transport and manufacturing costs go up across the board, pushing up prices for everyday items—bad for household budgets.
Higher global crude prices eventually translate to costlier fuel at Indian petrol pumps, increasing travel and logistics expenses for everyone.

watch_next: Official verifications or updates regarding the safety and operational status of Saudi Arabia's Ras Tanura refinery.
The upcoming EIA (U.S. Energy Information Administration) inventory report to confirm U.S. crude stockpile trends.
analysis.caveats: If subsequent reports confirm that Saudi oil facilities suffered no actual damage and operations remain fully normal, the supply fears could fade and oil prices might reverse.

analysis.tldr: New RBI rules on currency trading created confusion, making banks hesitant to deal in dollar-rupee contracts, which could affect how easily businesses manage foreign currency risks.
the_story: The Reserve Bank of India (RBI, India's central bank) issued clarifications on recent measures taken to support the rupee (the Indian currency).

The clarification follows concerns over tighter hedging rules (strategies to protect against currency price changes) and cash margins on certain derivatives (financial contracts whose value depends on another asset).

Several lenders (banks that lend money) have held back on quoting dollar-rupee forwards (contracts to buy or sell foreign currency at a fixed rate in the future) because of confusion over transaction requirements.
The RBI's earlier steps included redirecting oil companies' dollar purchases and levying cash reserve requirements, which raised uncertainties in financial markets.
analysis.what_happened: The Reserve Bank of India stepped in to clear up confusion caused by its recent rules aimed at supporting the rupee. Banks had stopped quoting certain currency contracts because they were unsure about the exact transaction requirements under the new guidelines.
analysis.analogy: It is like a traffic police introducing a strict new rule at a busy intersection without explaining it clearly, causing all the drivers to suddenly freeze and stop moving until the police officer gives clear hand signals.
why_it_matters_india: RBI introduces tighter rules and cash margins to support the rupee -> Banks get confused about transaction requirements
Banks hold back on quoting dollar-rupee forwards -> Businesses find it harder to lock in future exchange rates
Uncertainty rises in financial markets -> Overall market stability and foreign exchange liquidity get impacted
RBI issues official clarifications -> Banks gradually resume normal currency operations

impacts.rationale: Market uncertainties and hesitation by banks can put downward pressure on the currency, making imports slightly costlier for everyday items.

watch_next: Whether banks resume normal quoting of dollar-rupee forward contracts
Further updates or relaxations from the Reserve Bank of India regarding forex rules
analysis.caveats: The article text is brief and relies heavily on a single headline update, so the broader market fallout depends on how quickly banks interpret the new RBI clarifications.

analysis.tldr: Rising global energy prices could push up costs in India, as the US central bank keeps borrowing costs steady amid conflict fears.
the_story: The US Federal Reserve (the US central bank that sets interest rates) is widely expected to keep interest rates steady.
Rising energy prices linked to the Iran war are fueling inflation concerns (rising prices of everyday goods), while consumer prices accelerate and affordability comes under pressure.
Investors are watching comments from Chair Kevin Warsh for clues on the December rate decision and future monetary tightening (making borrowing costlier to cool down the economy).
analysis.what_happened: The US Federal Reserve is expected to keep its benchmark interest rate unchanged. This hesitation comes because conflict involving Iran is pushing up energy prices, driving up inflation concerns and consumer price pressures in the US.
analysis.analogy: It is like a shopkeeper refusing to lower prices because the cost of electricity and transport keeps climbing, making him worried about future expenses.
why_it_matters_india: Conflict involving Iran pushes up global energy and oil prices due to supply fears.
Higher global energy costs feed into overall inflation concerns and risk driving up import bills for energy-importing countries like India.
If US interest rates stay high because of inflation, global investors tend to keep their money in safer US assets rather than emerging markets.
This can create pressure on the Indian rupee and affect local market sentiment.

impacts.rationale: War involving Iran drives up global energy prices, which usually trickles down to costlier fuel at home — bad for household budgets.
Higher global inflation and steady US rates make the US dollar more attractive, causing the rupee to weaken, which makes imports costlier for India.
Global uncertainty and inflation worries can prompt foreign investors to pull money out of Indian stocks, creating short-term downward pressure.
Geopolitical conflicts like the war involving Iran trigger global safe-haven buying, raising gold prices, which makes jewelry costlier for buyers.

watch_next: Statements from US Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh regarding the December rate decision
Developments and updates surrounding the Iran war and energy supply chains
analysis.caveats: The article text is brief and heavily mixed with unrelated website promotions, meaning market reactions depend heavily on how the conflict unfolds.

analysis.analogy: It is like a group of local shop owners getting together to rewrite the rules of the neighborhood market so that small stores can compete fairly with the big supermarkets.

This can eventually influence jobs and revenues in export-heavy sectors.

events.headline: BYD expands EV shipping fleet as wars upend freight costs and key trade routes

items.title: BYD expands EV shipping fleet as wars upend freight costs and key trade routes
items.summary: The ''BYD Explorer No. 1'' car carrier, loaded with new energy vehicles, is setting sail from Yantai Port in Yantai, China, on January 10, 2024.

events.article_text:
China’s BYDiBYDBYD Auto is a Chinese carmaker that became the world’s leading EV manufacturer in 2023, competing with Tesla for market share and global attention.READ MORE is building cars faster than it can export, so it’s adding more ships.

The world’s largest electric vehicle maker will expand its fleet of car-carrying cargo ships to 18 from eight by 2029, according to shipping industry reports. Each new carrier will have the capacity to carry about 9,200 cars and will be built by China Merchants Industry.

Owning its fleet could cut BYD’s cost to ship each car abroad by as much as 40% compared with renting carriers, according to one industry estimate. BYD’s increasing export capacity could help it push further into global markets, intensifying competition for automakers including Tesla and traditional U.S. brands.

“Carmakers like BYD, which invested in the sector ahead of the surge, are reaping the rewards of that long-term strategy,” Andrea De Luca, a maritime analyst at Boston-based shipping data company Veson Nautical, told Rest of World. “By owning their ships, they can save money compared with chartering at today’s elevated rates, prioritize their most important markets, enter new ones more easily, and depend less on charter market swings.”

BYD did not respond to Rest of World’s request for comment.

In 2022, BYD announced a plan worth $687 million to build its own car carriers, to fix what founder Wang Chuanfu called a shortage of shipping capacity for exports. Between January 2024 and September 2025, the company put eight car carriers into service.

Earlier this year, BYD told investors that a shortage of shipping capacity had held back its exports. In September, the company sold 180,700 cars outside China, more than double a year ago and almost 40% of its monthly total sales.

Wars in the Red Sea and around the Strait of Hormuz have pushed up freight costs and forced ships onto longer routes around conflict zones. Renting a car carrier with capacity of about 6,500 cars now costs $95,000 a day, up from $50,000 in February, according to shipping data and analytics firm Clarksons Research. Chinese owners account for only about 10% of global car carrier capacity, including ships on order, so carmakers from the country hire ships from international shipping companies, the research arm of shipbroker Clarksons said.

With BYD aiming to sell more than 2.5 million cars overseas next year, up from a target of 1.9 to 2 million this year, owning a fleet cushions against higher shipping bills and gives more control over space and routes, analysts said.

2.5 million Number of cars BYD aims to sell overseas next year, up from a target of 1.9 to 2 million this year.

“The very strong growth in Chinese exports, fueling strong Asia-Europe fronthaul demand growth, is the biggest single factor behind the increase in charter rates,” Stephen Gordon, managing director of Clarksons Research, told Rest of World. “Additionally, conflict in the Middle East has caused regional disruption and inefficiencies, which have helped to further tighten markets after a two-year period of gradual normalization.”

Most car carriers on Asia-Europe routes are sailing around the Cape of Good Hope to avoid the Red Sea, adding about 25% to the distance and as many as 14 days to each voyage, De Luca said. With shipping through the Strait of Hormuz disrupted, the spot rate for moving cars from China to the Middle East has jumped to $220 per cubic meter of cargo space from $65 in February, he said.

In China, industrywide sales of EVs and plug-in hybrids fell 12% in the first eight months of the year, after the government cut tax breaks for buyers. BYD sold 33% fewer cars at home over the same period.

Many Chinese carmakers have kept their factories busy by selling surplus cars abroad as changes to tax and subsidy incentives have cooled demand at home, George Whitcombe, a senior EV analyst at London-based battery data provider Benchmark Mineral Intelligence, told Rest of World.

Exports of China-made EVs are now rising faster than their registrations overseas, pointing to a growing stock of unsold cars, he said.

“Control over its distribution network is a strategy BYD has long pursued,” Whitcombe said. “With other Chinese automakers left without their own fleet of ships and exposed to rising shipping costs, it potentially leaves them in a less competitive position to grow their overseas presence.”

Tesla, BYD’s main U.S. rival, has relied on other companies’ carriers to export from China. Its Shanghai plant shipped more cars abroad than it sold at home in the first eight months of the year. Carmakers that charter ships are more exposed to swings in the charter market than those that own them, De Luca said.

BYD’s giant carriers are mainly a marketing exercise, Felipe Munoz, founder of research platform Car Industry Analysis, told Rest of World. Owning ships has its drawbacks and advantages, he said.

“By displaying these massive carriers, it aims to project an image of power and speed to the rest of the world,” Munoz said. “It is more a political statement against the established carmakers by telling the world that BYD is moving fast and has a lot of resources to make the most advanced EVs.”

BYD’s fleet is about control, and extending into logistics is a natural step now that it exports millions of cars amid geopolitical volatility and cost swings, Lei Xing, founder of AutoXing, a Chinese auto industry consultancy, told Rest of World. BYD ships only EVs and plug-in hybrids, which need specially configured carriers, and most of its fleet runs on liquefied natural gas as ports tighten green-fuel rules, he said.

Rival Geely began running its first car carrier in 2025, on a long-term charter from London-based shipowner Zodiac Maritime. Chery set up a venture with Wuhu Shipyard in 2023 to build car carriers for its own fleet in eastern China.

“Geely, on the other hand, will be running its own ships eventually,” Lei Xing

analysis.tldr: Chinese electric vehicle makers cutting their shipping costs could intensify global competition, putting pressure on Indian electric vehicle makers and local transport pricing dynamics as global supply chains shift.
the_story: Chinese electric vehicle maker BYD is expanding its fleet of car-carrying cargo ships from eight to 18 by 2029, with each new carrier built by China Merchants Industry to hold about 9,200 cars.
Owning ships could cut BYD's shipping costs abroad by up to 40% compared to renting, protecting the company from surging freight rates caused by wars in the Red Sea and around the Strait of Hormuz.
Renting a car carrier has jumped from $50,000 a day in February to $95,000 a day, while longer voyages around the Cape of Good Hope add 14 days and 25% more distance to Asia-Europe routes.
BYD aims to sell over 2.5 million cars overseas next year, up from a target of 1.9 to 2 million this year, as falling domestic sales push Chinese automakers to export surplus cars.
Rival Chinese carmakers like Geely and Chery are also moving toward owning or controlling their own fleets, leaving competitors who rent ships more exposed to volatile shipping costs.
analysis.what_happened: Chinese electric vehicle maker BYD is aggressively expanding its private cargo ship fleet to bypass skyrocketing global shipping costs and port disruptions. Wars in the Middle East have forced cargo ships onto longer routes, driving daily rental rates for transport vessels up sharply and squeezing carmakers that rely on chartered ships.
analysis.analogy: It is like a local delivery shop buying its own delivery trucks to avoid paying massive, unpredictable fees to a third-party courier service every time fuel prices spike.
why_it_matters_india: Lower shipping costs for global electric vehicle giants like BYD help them price vehicles aggressively abroad.
Intense global competition from low-cost Chinese exports puts pressure on domestic Indian automotive companies looking to scale their own electric vehicle manufacturing.
Global shipping bottlenecks and rising freight rates can spill over into broader trade costs, affecting imported components for Indian manufacturing.
Cheaper overseas scaling by major global electric vehicle players indirectly influences pricing and competitive strategies for clean energy transport in developing markets like India.

impacts.rationale: Middle East conflicts and longer voyages around the Cape of Good Hope keep transport costs elevated, which is bad for general import-heavy trade.
Aggressive export pushes by Chinese manufacturers increase pricing pressure on rivals worldwide, a mixed signal for consumers but tough for legacy makers.

watch_next: Whether other major international carmakers adopt private shipping fleets to combat high logistics costs
Updates on Middle Eastern shipping route safety and freight charter prices
analysis.caveats: The article focuses entirely on Chinese manufacturing and global maritime routes, meaning direct impacts on Indian domestic stocks will depend heavily on local government policy and trade tariffs.

events.headline: Farmers prepare for low rain but get floods instead

items.title: Farmers prepare for low rain but get floods instead
items.summary: “At the Krishi Vigyan Kendra in July, we were told to plant more sesame, groundnut and urad. These are crops expected to withstand less rain. But God decided to flood our fields instead,” shares Jaidevi, a farmer in Chandpura, a village in Mahoba, Uttar Pradesh, pointing to her withered sesame crop. Jaidevi and her husband […]

events.article_text:
If you liked this story, share it with other people.

“At the Krishi Vigyan Kendra in July, we were told to plant more sesame, groundnut and urad. These are crops expected to withstand less rain. But God decided to flood our fields instead,” shares Jaidevi, a farmer in Chandpura, a village in Mahoba, Uttar Pradesh, pointing to her withered sesame crop. Jaidevi and her husband own three bighas of farmland and have struggled to make a living from it. Chandpura is among the worst hit villages by intense rainfall in Mahoba during this southwest monsoon.

Ahead of the 2026 southwest monsoon, Mahoba’s Krishi Vigyan Kendra advised farmers to sow low-water crops, anticipating low rainfall because of the effects of El Niño this year. The monsoon arrived nearly 20 days late, with deficient rainfall for much of the season that typically starts mid-June. But the pattern reversed in late August, when heavy rain lashed the region, leaving much of farmland waterlogged by September 15.

This year’s El Niño forecast is expected to be one of the strongest on record. Its impact in India is in the form of a weaker monsoon and warmer temperatures. In June, the agriculture ministry classified Mahoba as one of 111 high-priority districts based on irrigation coverage and vulnerability to rainfall deficits. Irrigation coverage in these districts is expected to be below 25 percent.

Part of the drought-prone Bundelkhand region, Mahoba has long faced rainfall deficits, falling groundwater levels and limited irrigation. This monsoon though, Mahoba received 1,127 mm of rainfall between June 1 and September 30, about 90% above its normal rainfall of 588.4 mm, according to the India Meteorological Department (IMD).

Trends from rest of the state showed that Uttar Pradesh recorded its highest monsoon rainfall in 18 years, said Atul Kumar Singh, a scientist at IMD Lucknow. However, the rest of the country showed an opposite trend. India received 759.4 mm of rainfall (June to September), its fourth-lowest monsoon rainfall since 2001 and the 13th lowest since 1901. The impact of El Niño was felt across several states, with the Centre declaring drought in five states, including Maharashtra, Rajasthan and Telangana.

For farmers in UP including Mahoba, the excess rain came at the wrong time. Standing kharif crops were submerged and damaged in the fields. “We were supposed to harvest our kharif crop in October, but now we know it will yield nothing. The entire crop has rotted,” says Sampat, another farmer, standing in the fields with her husband. The couple, both in their late fifties, had high fever but continued working because they saw no other option for their income.

The Indian Council of Agricultural Research-Agricultural Technology Application Research Institute (ICAR-ATARI) contingency plan for the season had also advised farmers to prepare for the expected effects of El Niño, including below-normal rainfall. These plans are usually shared with KVKs and their officials then communicate the information to farmers through meetings at the centres, discussions with village sarpanches, and sometimes verbally in the villages. But this season brought a sharp shift in weather conditions, exposing the limits of planning in a changing climate.

The damage was not limited to pulses and sesame; vegetable cultivation was also severely affected by the flooding. Jag Kushwaha, who owns 13 bighas in Bijapur, another village hit by heavy rain, struggled to hold back tears while showing his cucumber fields. In one field, he says, some fruit survived. In the other, there was not even a flower.

Kushwaha estimates that under favourable conditions, he earned approximately ₹80,000 from a half-hectare cucumber field. This year, he is unsure whether he will recover even his cultivation costs. Eleven members of his family depend on farming. Without the rain damage, he says, the crop would have generated enough income to support his family for the next two to three months.

For farmers in Mahoba, the problem is not simply excessive rain. It is also the widening gap between seasonal forecasts and localised weather events, making it harder to plan according to the crop calendar.

“Climate change is a regular phenomenon, but in recent years it has been accelerated primarily owing to anthropogenic activities, modifying complex interactions between different components of the Earth system. This makes forecasting challenging at different spatial and temporal scales,” explains Atul Kumar Singh, a scientist from IMD Lucknow.

Seasonal forecasts can indicate broad rainfall patterns over a larger area and longer period, but they cannot always capture where and when an extreme rainfall event will occur. This matters for farmers whose decisions depend on the timing and intensity of rain.

Explaining why the uncertainty is particularly significant in Bundelkhand, Raghwendra Singh, the director of ICAR-ATARI, says western Uttar Pradesh has better irrigation facilities, whereas eastern Uttar Pradesh and Bundelkhand remain vulnerable to rainfall deficits, particularly during critical crop growth stages. This vulnerability has pushed authorities to focus more on water management and crop planning suited to variable rainfall.

Seasonal indicators may have pointed towards a weaker monsoon, but they could not account for the intense rainfall that arrived later in Mahoba, he adds.

The rain turned the farmland into lakes and has destroyed an estimated 70-80% of standing crops in some affected areas. Considering the situation, Mahoba district magistrate Ghazal Bharadwaj announced on September 12 that support would be provided under the Pradhan Mantri Fasal Bima Yojana (PMFBY) within 30 days. The Agriculture Department, crop insurance company (IFFCO-TOKIO General Insurance Company Limited) and Revenue Department will prepare a consolidated report, which may take until the end of November to finalise.

But there is another concern for tenant farmers, who may struggl

analysis.tldr: Crop damage from unexpected floods in Uttar Pradesh and droughts in other states could raise vegetable and food prices in local markets, impacting your monthly household budget.
the_story: Farmers in Mahoba, Uttar Pradesh, were advised by the local Krishi Vigyan Kendra to plant low-water crops like sesame, groundnut, and urad because scientists anticipated a weak monsoon due to El Niño.

Instead of low rain, Mahoba received 1,127 mm of rainfall between June 1 and September 30, which is about 90% above its normal rainfall of 588.4 mm, according to the India Meteorological Department (IMD).
The heavy rain arrived late in the season, waterlogging farmlands by September 15 and destroying standing kharif crops (summer-sown crops harvested in autumn) and vegetables like cucumbers.

Nationwide, the impact of El Niño created a mixed picture: India received its fourth-lowest monsoon rainfall since 2001, prompting the Centre to declare drought in five states including Maharashtra, Rajasthan, and Telangana.

Mahoba district magistrate Ghazal Bharadwaj announced on September 12 that support would be provided under the Pradhan Mantri Fasal Bima Yojana [PMFBY - a government crop insurance scheme] within 30 days, with a final report expected by November.
analysis.what_happened: Weather forecasters expected a weak monsoon and drought across India because of El Niño (a warming of ocean surface waters that usually brings less rain to India). Farmers in Mahoba, Uttar Pradesh, planted crops that need less water based on this advice. However, the weather pattern suddenly reversed in late August, bringing heavy floods that destroyed their harvests.
analysis.analogy: It is like packing only heavy woollens because the weather department predicted a freezing winter, only for a massive heatwave to hit and ruin all your clothes.
why_it_matters_india: Unexpected heavy rains in some regions and droughts in others destroy harvests of pulses, oilseeds, and vegetables.
Lower crop supplies lead to higher food prices in local wholesale and retail markets.
Higher food prices push up overall retail inflation (the rate at which prices for everyday goods rise).
Struggling farmers earn less income, reducing their spending power and affecting rural demand for consumer goods.

impacts.rationale: Damaged crops and vegetable supplies mean pricier food items in grocery stores, which is bad for everyday household budgets.

impacts.target: Food and vegetable prices in local markets
impacts.rationale: With local farms losing 70-80% of standing crops and ruined cucumber yields, scarcer produce pushes up costs for consumers.

impacts.target: Rural consumption and demand for consumer goods
impacts.rationale: When farmers lose their income to rotted crops, they spend less money, which can slow down rural sales for companies selling bikes, soaps, and clothes.

watch_next: The final damage assessment report by the Agriculture Department and IFFCO-TOKIO General Insurance due by the end of November
Government updates on crop insurance payouts under the Pradhan Mantri Fasal Bima Yojana
analysis.caveats: The article text cuts off at the end regarding tenant farmers, but the core reporting on Mahoba's rainfall data and crop loss is fully documented.

events.headline: Asia’s forced labour bans should fix abuses, not just block goods

items.title: Asia’s forced labour bans should fix abuses, not just block goods
items.summary: Import restrictions can pressure suppliers to clean up their act, but only if there is a clear route back to compliance.

events.article_text:
An abrupt contract cancellation could leave workers unpaid and out of work (Yutao Chou/Unsplash)

Import restrictions can pressure suppliers to clean up their act, but only if there is a clear route back to compliance.

Asia’s forced labour bans should fix abuses, not just block goods

Governments across Asia are banning imports produced using forced labour. Under pressure from Washington’s Section 301 forced labour investigations (Opens in new window), India (Opens in new window), Cambodia (Opens in new window), and Sri Lanka (Opens in new window) are among the countries that have adopted prohibitions this year. The bans raise a difficult question for buyers who find forced labour in their supply chain: should they walk away or fix it?

In 2021, the International Labour Organisation estimated (Opens in new window) that 27.6 million people were in forced labour worldwide, with more than half located in the Asia-Pacific region. Forced labour indicators (Opens in new window) include physical violence, intimidation, restricted movement, and withheld wages, among many others. For workers in forced labour, what matters most is fixing these abuses, not banning the goods they produce.

Import bans may be well intended, but they can also push companies to “cut and run” when forced labour is discovered, rather than undertake the hard work to remediate it. An abrupt contract cancellation could leave workers unpaid and out of work. This is why responsible business guidelines (Opens in new window) often treat ending a business relationship as a last resort after remediation efforts have failed. While enforcement (Opens in new window) of forced labour regulations is critical, Asian governments must also be mindful of adverse impacts (Opens in new window) on workers. Different approaches to this problem are emerging throughout the region.

India illustrates one approach. In July, India added a paragraph (2.20B (Opens in new window)) to its foreign trade policy (Opens in new window) to prohibit imports made, in whole or in part, using forced labour. However, neither the amendment nor the accompanying Handbook of Procedures (Opens in new window) addresses repaying affected workers. They also do not specify how a supplier’s products might return to good standing once abuses are fixed, which could reduce incentives to engage in remediation.

By contrast, Malaysia’s experience shows that a route back to good standing matters. Since 2019, US detention orders against Malaysian palm oil and glove makers have set conditions for lifting them. Meeting those conditions has helped return (Opens in new window) more than US$85 million in withheld wages and recruitment fees to workers.

A harvest from a palm oil plantation outside Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia (Nafise Motlaq/World Bank)

Several draft bills throughout the Asia-Pacific illustrate another approach, which focuses on corporate responsibility in supply chains. Precise obligations will depend on adopted provisions, but this model is instructive. For example, Thailand has considered (Opens in new window) a responsible business conduct law that would require all large companies operating in the country to identify risks across their supply chains and, critically, remediate abuses when they occur.

South Korea has explored options with a similar logic. Under a proposed (Opens in new window) law, buyers could end supplier relationships over serious ongoing abuse, but they must consider the potential harm of cutting ties abruptly.

An import ban can give governments leverage, but it is most effective when combined with a duty to remediate abuses. Asian policymakers should consider three recommendations.

For workers in forced labour, what matters most is fixing these abuses, not banning the goods they produce.

First, laws should require good faith efforts to remediate (Opens in new window) findings of abuse before suppliers are dropped. Termination of a supplier relationship should be reserved (Opens in new window) for cases where remediation has failed, or the abuse is severe and ongoing. Asian nations, such as through ASEAN, should agree to a shared remediation standard and recognise one another’s verified results. This could include a reasonable deadline for remediation, to eliminate incentives for indefinite delay.

Second, laws should also require buyers that suspend orders help pay for the remediation. Suspension is often presented as a middle path between staying and leaving, but it can also deprive suppliers of the revenue they need to eliminate abuses. Establishing requirements for a fund financed by buyers proportionate to their share of the supplier’s output could cover lost wages while orders are on hold.

Third, the conditions for lifting import bans should be clear. Once there is independent confirmation that abuse has ended, including workers being paid in full, goods should be able to re-enter the market. As with remediation standards, common conditions could be set across nations so that the same relief applies to all suppliers. Publishing these conditions in advance would give suppliers a clear incentive to fix abuses rather than conceal them.

These recommendations alone will not eliminate forced labour; auditors face their own challenges (Opens in new window), and often miss abuse. Buyers will likely resist costs and push them down to suppliers where possible. Cooperation across jurisdictions is also critical, but difficult to coordinate and maintain. Any conditions for lifting bans must guard against loopholes. These challenges, however, are not reasons to avoid the problem of remediating forced labour.

Asia’s emerging import bans have made forced labour much harder to ignore. But these rules must consider the workers subjected to forced labour, not just the goods they produce. Import bans must be accompanied by clear requirements for remediation, mechanisms to pay for it, and routes for lifting bans where warranted. Failing to do so may stop pr

analysis.tldr: New rules banning forced-labour imports could disrupt Indian supply chains and exports if they do not provide clear ways to fix problems instead of just cutting off trade.
the_story: Governments across Asia, including India under pressure from Washington's Section 301 forced labour investigations, are adopting prohibitions against imports produced using forced labour.
In July, India added a paragraph (2.20B) to its foreign trade policy to prohibit imports made using forced labour.
India's current amendment and Handbook of Procedures do not address repaying affected workers or specify how suppliers can return to good standing once abuses are fixed.
The International Labour Organisation estimated in 2021 that 27.6 million people were in forced labour worldwide, with over half in the Asia-Pacific region.
analysis.what_happened: Governments across Asia are introducing import bans on goods made with forced labour, driven partly by US investigations. India adopted this rule in July by updating its foreign trade policy. However, the current rules lack clear paths for suppliers to fix issues and get back into business.
analysis.analogy: It is like a school banning a snack brand because of a quality issue at the factory, but refusing to tell the factory owner what changes to make so they can sell snacks again.
why_it_matters_india: India banned imports made with forced labour in its foreign trade policy.
Without clear rules on how to fix problems, Indian suppliers caught in violations might lose business abruptly rather than being helped to correct issues.
This can cut off revenue for local factories, leaving vulnerable workers unpaid and out of work.
Export supply chains may face higher compliance costs and stricter scrutiny from global buyers.

impacts.rationale: Stricter import bans without clear correction paths could disrupt supply chains, which is generally bad for local businesses and employment.

watch_next: Whether Indian authorities update their Handbook of Procedures to include clear ways for suppliers to fix violations and lift bans
How major global buyers enforce supply chain compliance in South Asia
analysis.caveats: Only the article text was used, and actual economic impacts will depend on how strictly these trade policies are enforced by India and its trading partners.

events.headline: Import Licensing Committee addresses notifications, trade concerns, transparency efforts

items.title: Import Licensing Committee addresses notifications, trade concerns, transparency efforts
items.summary: At its 15 October meeting, the WTO Committee on Import Licensing examined challenges for WTO members in preparing notifications, including findings from a recent WTO workshop for government officials. It also reviewed the latest information on members' notification practices. In addition, the Committee considered a range of trade concerns and reflected on lessons from recent experience-sharing sessions aimed at strengthening communication, public-private engagement and access to information on import licensing procedures.

events.article_text:
This note has been prepared by the WTO Secretariat to assist public understanding about the work of the WTO's councils, committees and other bodies. It is not intended as a complete account of all issues raised at the meeting. These can be found in the formal meeting minutes.

At the meeting, the WTO Secretariat presented the findings of a survey conducted among participants in the Workshop on Import Licensing and Notifications, held in September 2026, highlighting the practical challenges faced by participants in preparing notifications. Some 68% of respondents reported difficulties obtaining information from the responsible authorities. For the annual questionnaire, 72% cited difficulties obtaining up-to-date information, while 48% reported challenges identifying all relevant licensing and similar administrative procedures.

Regarding possible improvements, respondents highlighted clearer responsibilities among authorities (52%) and the designation of a national focal point (44%), alongside stronger inter-agency coordination, regular reporting of changes to licensing procedures, practical guidance and examples, and further technical assistance. The findings suggest that the main challenges arise before drafting, particularly in identifying relevant procedures and gathering current information. The survey permitted multiple responses, and its findings reflect participants' experiences rather than those of the WTO membership as a whole.

The Chair, Ms Mi Jin Ryu (Republic of Korea), informed members that since the last Committee meeting in June, a total of 49 notifications have been received under various provisions of the Agreement on Import Licensing. Of these, 16 were received after the close of the meeting agenda and will be reviewed at the next Committee meeting.

Of the 33 notifications reviewed at the 15 October meeting, 23 notifications were submitted under Article 7.3 of the Agreement. Article 7.3 requires members to complete the annual questionnaire on import licensing procedures promptly and in full.

Regarding the annual questionnaire, the Chair noted that 21 members have never submitted any reply to the questionnaire since joining the WTO. In addition, 11 members have never submitted any notifications under the Agreement on Import Licensing. She encouraged these members to take the first step or contact the WTO Secretariat for technical assistance.

The Committee addressed follow-up questions regarding two previously raised trade concerns at the 15 October meeting. These comprised one from Brazil concerning the submission of due diligence statements under the European Union Deforestation Regulation and the other from Japan regarding import restrictions in Indonesia on various products, including electric products, steel products and fabrics.

The Committee then addressed 14 trade concerns regarding import licensing regimes of various products. Two of these concerns were raised for the first time, while the others were raised at the Committee's previous meeting in June 2026 or at earlier meetings. The trade concerns cover:

The Chair noted that the Committee has undertaken a number of initiatives to further improve transparency, with the active involvement of members and the assistance of the Secretariat. These initiatives include the organization of two experience-sharing sessions bringing together representatives from the public and private sectors.

The first experience-sharing session took place in April 2025 and focused on "Overcoming Roadblocks to Notifications". Building on the sustained interest and engagement of members, a second experience-sharing session was organized on 4 June 2026, this time with the participation of private-sector representatives.

Entitled "Enhancing Transparency and Trade Predictability through Effective Notification Practices, Public-Private Collaboration, and Digitalization of Import Licensing Procedures," the second session provided an opportunity for participants to exchange practical experiences and perspectives on the challenges associated with import licensing procedures and their impact on traders and businesses.

The Chair said the presentations and subsequent exchanges highlighted three closely related areas for further consideration: first, improving notification practices; second, strengthening the communication and accessibility of information; and third, enhancing interaction among members and with the private sector.

Seven members took the floor to comment. The Chair said the interventions showed members valued this kind of experience sharing. She added that the Secretariat would compile all the suggestions made and that she would hold an informal meeting to see how to move forward.

The Chair said the next Committee meeting is tentatively scheduled for 22 April 2027.

Problems viewing this page? If so, please contact [email protected] giving details of the operating system and web browser you are using.

analysis.tldr: Global trade rules are facing transparency hurdles, which could eventually influence how smoothly Indian goods enter foreign markets.
the_story: At a WTO Import Licensing Committee meeting on 15 October, survey findings showed 68% of respondents struggled to get information from authorities, and 72% faced issues getting up-to-date information for annual questionnaires.
The Chair, Ms Mi Jin Ryu of the Republic of Korea, reported that 49 notifications were received since June, with 33 reviewed at the meeting.
The Chair highlighted that 21 members have never replied to the annual questionnaire since joining the WTO, and 11 members have never submitted notifications.

The Committee discussed trade concerns, including a Brazilian concern about European Union deforestation rules and a Japanese concern over Indonesian import restrictions on electric products, steel, and fabrics, plus 14 concerns regarding import licensing regimes.
analysis.what_happened: The World Trade Organization's Import Licensing Committee met to discuss transparency issues in global trade rules. Officials reviewed survey results showing that countries struggle to gather up-to-date information and submit required reports, while also addressing specific trade complaints raised by Brazil, Japan, and other members.
analysis.analogy: It is like a group of shopkeepers agreeing to post their store prices clearly on a public bulletin board, but many shopkeepers keep forgetting or hiding their price lists, making it hard for customers to know what the rules are.
why_it_matters_india: WTO committees discuss trade rules and licensing barriers that affect how nations restrict or allow imports.
Delays or lack of transparency in global import procedures can create hurdles for Indian exporters trying to sell goods abroad.
Discussions on regulations like EU deforestation rules or foreign import restrictions can set precedents affecting Indian shipments of steel, fabrics, and electronics.
Smoother global trade transparency generally helps lower unpredictable costs for international businesses, though this meeting itself only addressed administrative reporting.

impacts.rationale: Unrelated administrative discussions at the WTO have no direct bearing on software export earnings.
Global trade committee updates do not shift safe-haven demand or domestic bullion prices.
Bureaucratic procedural meetings at the WTO are too distant from corporate earnings to move the broader stock market.

watch_next: Future WTO committee meetings scheduled for April 2027
Updates on how countries resolve specific import licensing and deforestation regulation concerns
analysis.caveats: This meeting focused entirely on administrative procedures and transparency workshops rather than binding trade penalties or tariff changes.

history.title: The bubble that took thirty years to repay
history.what: At its 1989 peak the Tokyo stock market was worth more than the American one, and the land under the Imperial Palace was said to be worth more than all of California. The Nikkei then fell about 80% and did not regain its 1989 high until 2024 — thirty-five years later.
history.why: The 1985 Plaza Accord pushed the yen sharply higher, hurting exporters. The Bank of Japan cut rates hard to compensate, and the cheap money went into land and shares rather than into business investment. Banks lent against property using property as collateral, so rising prices justified more lending, which raised prices further. A closed loop, and everyone inside it could point to a rational-sounding reason.
history.impact: Households and banks spent two decades repairing balance sheets instead of spending and lending. Growth flatlined, prices actually fell for years, and a generation entered a frozen job market. Japan's share of world output fell from roughly 15% to under 5%.
history.policy: Rates went to zero and later below it. Japan invented quantitative easing in 2001 — a central bank creating money to buy government bonds — because conventional rate cuts had run out of room. Banks were eventually forced to recognise bad loans instead of rolling them over.
history.consequence: Every major central bank used Japan's playbook in 2008 and again in 2020, which is why zero rates and bond-buying stopped being exotic. Japan also proved an economy can stagnate for decades without a dramatic collapse — the danger is not always a crash.
history.pattern: When an asset is bought with debt secured against that same asset, the cycle feeds itself upward and then downward with equal force. Ask what the collateral is; if the collateral is the thing being bought, you are looking at the mechanism.
history.india_echo: Indian property lending and promoter share-pledging are the same shape on a smaller scale. It is why the RBI watches loan-to-value ratios, and why a promoter pledging shares to buy more shares deserves real suspicion.
history.watch_for: Lending growth running far ahead of income growth, with the asset itself as the security. That combination has never ended gently.
